While the plot event of the mother's heatstroke is heavily foreshadowed, the emotional turns and revelations at the end of the story are both surprising and completely earned. 

First, when the son returns to the empty house five weeks later, he discovers that she has preserved the artifacts of his visit like a shrine: his washed mug is still in the drying rack, the crossword puzzle they worked on is still on the arm of the chair, and the water glass is still on the windowsill. Even more surprisingly, on the saved gin rummy score sheet, she has secretly added a note blaming him for leaving ("To be continued") and added fifteen extra points to her own score behind his back. This is an unexpected comedic and emotional beat, yet it is entirely appropriate for a woman already established as stubbornly unsentimental on the surface and an unabashed cheater at cards.

Second, the final revelation that the straw hat she refused to wear for twenty years has her name written inside the band by her late husband is a surprising twist. In hindsight, it is deeply appropriate, instantly contextualizing why she claimed the hat was "for show" and refused to let it get ruined in the sun.
